THE IDEA: the illusions are played BY THE BAND, not by a pad behind it.
- THE STAIR (0:19): a line over the low chug climbs the scale an octave every bar and never gets higher. Four guitars a side play it an octave apart, each fading in at the bottom and out at the top. Every bar is the same bar; every bar starts higher than the last.
- THE TURN (1:17): the low chug at three speeds at once, all speeding up; the fastest fades out as a slower one fades in. Faster and faster, never faster. The kit holds the bar, and every fourth bar line they are together again.
- THE DESCENT (1:55): the stair downwards and all of it: the whole riff a step lower every bar. A tuning that keeps dropping.
- THE POLE (2:53): a breath. One chord through a filter that climbs for ever, and a bass that is only its overtones.
- BOTH (3:22): pitch and speed rise together, like a tape speeding up, under a riser that never arrives. It stops dead.
- THE SUMMIT (4:02): a bar of nothing, then the first bars again, exactly. After all that climbing the band is where it started.

WHY. 'Both' is the song's last illusion: pitch and speed rise together, 'as a tape speeding up does'. A tape that speeds up takes the cymbals with it. Here the drummer's right hand kept plain eighths on the china for the whole passage, 300 ms apart from first stroke to last, while six guitars sped up round it: the one part in the passage saying that nothing is getting faster. (Harry on the turn, 17 Nov: 'Faster and faster'.)

The china plays the riff's own strokes at all three of the guitars' speeds, each under the same bell as its guitar: one voice fading in from half speed (462 ms apart, to 307), one doubling at full level (295 ms to 152: the eighth becomes the sixteenth), one from the sixteenth towards the thirty-second as it fades out (149 ms to 86). v30, HALF WAY ROUND (section w7, the pole, 2:52.8-3:16.8; no section round had focused it). Ten notes on a part that was already in the song; no guitar, lead, wheel, bass or drum note changes. LISTEN FOR 2:52.8: under the chord and the three climbing leads, a plain held tone: F for a bar, then B for a bar, and round, ten bars, until the run out at 3:16.8.
WHY. In the pole the three leads climb the stair's line at half an octave a bar, so their bars begin on F, B, F, B: the two notes of the song's scale that are half an octave apart. Half an octave is the one step that is exactly as far up as it is down, and the song's plain tone (a Shepard tone: every octave of a note at once) has no height to settle which. Two such tones half an octave apart are the textbook case where listeners disagree about which is the higher. In a song called False Summit that is the title's question in its plainest form: which of the two is the top? The tone had been silent in the pole since v12 gave its line to the leads. Harry on the stair: "It climbed better with the tone under it".
WHAT IT PLAYS. One held note a bar on the tone's own track, F at 2:52.8, B at 2:55.2, and so on to the B at 3:14.4: a stair with two steps. Under the leads, which go up the scale between the two, it should be heard to climb half an octave every bar and be back where it was every second bar; by itself it would only rock. So the tone now runs through the song: alone at the foot, under the stair, down the descent (v28), half way round at the pole, and up the run out of it into 'both'.
MEASURED, THE TONE ALONE (raw, seed 0). On F its two loudest octaves, 349 and 698 Hz, are within 0.4 to 3.0 dB of each other (which is louder changes with the bar); on B the loudest is 494 Hz, between them, with 988 Hz 1.5 to 2.3 under it and 247 Hz 5.0 to 6.3 under. So from F the ear can go up a tritone from 349 or down a tritone from 698 to the same B: the step is as ambiguous on this patch as it is on paper.
MEASURED, IN THE POLE (raw, seed 0, bar by bar, K). The tone stands 12.7 to 13.7 dB under everything else on its B bars and 14.1 to 15.6 under on its F bars; 6.6 to 8.3 dB under the three leads. THE COST, against the eleven records (finished files, seeds 0 / 11). The tone is 37% of the pole's 250-500 Hz, and that band reads +2.0 -> +3.9 and +1.3 -> +3.4 over the ten bars: +1.2 -> +3.6 and +0.4 -> +3.1 on F (2:52.8), +3.5 -> +4.8 and +2.0 -> +3.9 on A flat and E flat (3:02.4), 0.0 -> +2.2 and +1.2 -> +2.6 under the riser (3:12). EVERYTHING ELSE IS v29's: the master gives every other bar 0.008 dB less (not re-fitted), and gain-matched the foot, the stair, the turn, the descent, 'both' and the summit null at -65 dB on both seeds. WHY. Harry's brief for this song: "really make it a clear illusory song, all about the illusions". WHAT HE SAYS, AND WHAT IT TURNS INTO. "We have been here before" is true of the saying itself the second time and truer each time; the fifth saying is over the pole's first chord come back; and the song ends where it began. LISTEN FOR 2:43.2, best on headphones. Until now the eight guitars fell together there, a step of the scale on every accent of the riff. Now they split: one side goes on falling while the other climbs the same six notes, and FROM STEP TO STEP THE TWO SIDES CHANGE PLACES (they share the two notes where the lines meet). Two bars, the scale twice, 0.45 s and 0.3 s a step; then the run into the quiet middle, as before.
WHY. The song is "all about the illusions" and has collected them: of pitch (the stair), of speed (the turn), of both at once, the root that is not there, half way round, speech that turns to song. It had none of PLACE. The best known of those is Diana Deutsch's scale illusion (1973): a scale going down and the same scale going up, played together, with every other note of each sent to the other ear. Each ear is given a line that leaps about. What most listeners hear is two smooth lines, one on each side. Tchaikovsky wrote the opening of the last movement of his sixth symphony that way: neither violin section plays the tune the hall hears.
THIS SONG ALREADY HAD THE TWO SCALES. At 2:24 (v21) the right-hand guitars climb the six notes while the left go on falling, two steps a bar; at 2:38.4 they meet and fall together, three steps a bar, then six. So the material for the illusion was nineteen seconds away from where it belongs: the six-a-bar bars are the only place the fall moves at the speed the illusion is known at.
WHAT IS WRITTEN, two bars, each side four guitars an octave apart under the stair's bell as always:
   the LEFT plays   F  G flat  C  B  A flat  E flat   (both, climb, fall, both, fall, climb), twice
   the RIGHT plays  F  E flat  A flat  B  C  G flat   (both, fall, climb, both, climb, fall), twice
So the fall is on the right, then the left; after the meeting on B on the left, then the right; and each side leaps between the upper and the lower half of the octave at every step, which is how Deutsch's two ears were fed.
Nobody plays the fall (F, E flat, C, B, A flat, G flat) and nobody plays the climb. Each is whole only in the two sides together. The two lines are the fall's own ladder walked both ways from where the fall stands at 2:43.2, so they meet on B in the middle of each bar and on F at each bar line, and the six steps between them are thirds, sixths and unisons, as at 2:24. Up two octaves and down two are the whole wheel apart, so at 2:48 every string is on the note it would have fallen to and the run starts as it did. The two basses, the tone (v28) and the kick keep the fall under it: the ground does not change sides.
MEASURED (raw bench, own seed, the eight guitars alone; in each ear and at each step, the level of the falling note's pitch class against the climbing note's, every octave):
- THE EXCHANGE IS IN THE SOUND: in the left ear the climb stands 5.6 dB OVER the fall on the steps where the left has the climb and 5.1 UNDER it where it has the fall; in the right ear 5.7 over and 7.8 under (medians of the eight steps where the two lines differ). In v33 the fall stood 5 to 9 dB over the climb's notes in both ears throughout (medians; nobody played them: that is what an eight-guitar chord leaves on other notes); with the two stairs NOT exchanged (benched: the right climbs, the left falls, as at 2:24) the left ear holds the fall by 5 and the right the climb by 6 to 8 throughout.
- BOTH EARS SUMMED, the two lines are level (climb less fall -1.3 dB, median): in mono it is the two stairs in contrary motion and the exchange cannot be heard at all. That is the test of whether the illusion is doing anything: on one speaker, v34 and the unexchanged bench are the same music.
- LEVEL: the two bars 0.06 dB up (K, raw), the guitars alone 0.21; 120-250 Hz +0.5, nothing else over 0.2. Finished files, seeds 0 / 11 / 1: the two bars +0.09 / +0.07 / +0.02, each ear within 0.13 dB of v33, the mono sum within 0.10.
- THE REST OF THE SONG is v33's within 0.003 dB on three seeds (residual -66 dB or lower; the run's first quarter beat differs by the tails of the last step). The target is not moved.
THE COSTS: the steepest point of the fall is no longer the whole band falling as one: half of the guitars at any moment are going UP, and the fall there rests on the basses, the tone and one side. On speakers in a room the sides blur and it is the two stairs again, faster, which the song already has at 2:24. Each side alone is a tune of leaps with a tritone in it (G flat to C, C to G flat). The guitars are panned 0.7 either way, not hard: one side alone reads 10.4 dB lower in the far ear, so each ear has the other side in it already; Deutsch's listeners had none.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: all of what matters. Whether an ear hears a fall and a climb, or two jagged tunes, or a blur; on which side each line seems to be (Deutsch's listeners put the higher notes in one ear and the lower in the other, but these are guitars in four octaves under a bell, where higher and lower are not defined: the stair's own trick); whether six steps a bar is too fast for distorted chugs to be followed as lines at all.

The change is its last six bars, 2:09.6-2:24: thirteen notes on a new last track. No other note, track, fader or bus changes). Not checked by ear; everything below is measured or reasoned.

WHY. The descent is "the stair, downwards, and all of it", and one by one the stair's things have been given their mirror there: its tone (chirper-alpha, v28), the kit that changes gear (v10), the tom fill that never arrives (v5), the two sides going opposite ways (v21). One had none: THE LEAD. In the stair (v4) it is "the one honest line": over a climb that is never higher, one guitar really comes down two octaves, F5 to F3, a note to the half bar. And the fall's first twelve bars had no line at all: one note a bar on eight guitars.

WHAT. The same guitar answers itself. Over the fall that is never lower it really climbs: the same thirteen notes backwards, F3 to F5, the same twelve half bars and the short thirteenth on the bar line. Nothing was moved to fit it; the song already had the place:
- it comes in at bar 54 (2:09.6), where the fall has gone round once and is on F again, on the low F it landed on in the stair;
- the two tom fills that never land (v5: eight strokes into bar 54, twelve into bar 60) already stand at its two ends, each with a crash, as chirper-three's fills (v23) stand at the ends of the lead's first octave in the stair;
- it reaches its top F at bar 60 (2:24), on the bar line where the fall steepens and the right-hand guitars begin a climb of their own (v21): the lead hands them the way up, as in the stair it hands the way down to the guitars' run;
- it climbs two steps of the scale a bar and the band falls one, so on every second bar line they are on one note: F, C, A flat, F.
So the honest line has gone down two octaves and come back up two and is where it began, by walking. The band gets back to where it began by never having left. The notes are read from the lead's own, so whoever changes the lead changes its answer.
